https://www.politico.eu/article/francois.text: PARIS — Former French Prime Minister François Fillon has been suspended for 10 years from the Légion d’honneur , France’s highest order of merit, after being found guilty of providing his wife with a fake job in which she was paid a salary using taxpayer money. The decision to suspend Fillon was published Thursday morning in the French official gazette . It was approved by President Emmanuel Macron after being recommended by the body tasked with handling disciplinary measures for the Légion d’honneur . The fake jobs scandal emerged during the campaign for the 2017 presidential election and cost Fillon a shot at the presidency, as he was a front-runner in the contest before the allegations emerged. Advertisement Advertisement Fillon was found guilty in 2020 but appealed the decision. He and his wife Penelope, however, could not provide evidence that she had actually worked for her husband over the course of several contracts under which she was hired to be his parliamentary assistant during his time as an MP. The appeals court last year upheld the verdict, handing him a four-year suspended prison sentence and a €375,000 fine. The 72-year-old did not appeal that decision to a higher court. Former President Nicolas Sarkozy, under whom Fillon served, was also stripped of his Légion d’honneur last year after being found guilty of corruption and exhausting all his appeals. Sarkozy is fighting his conviction in another case for receiving money from Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi to fund his first presidential run in 2007. A first court found him guilty and sentenced him to five years in prison, but he has appealed the verdict and continues to profess his innocence.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/10/the-.text: Russian airports temporarily closed 993 times in August — an average of 32 times a day — as Ukrainian drone operations forced repeated airspace shutdowns across the country.Industry data shows it was the most disruptive month for Russian civil aviation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in early 2022.Figures from aviation security firm Osprey Flight Solutions state that restrictions were imposed at 32 airports in August, including Moscow and St Petersburg.Over the summer as a whole, 2,182 closures were recorded — already exceeding the full-year total for 2025.The Insider, an investigative Russian outlet, calculated that the August closures reached more than six times the 2025 monthly average.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines and insurers on 1 September that Russian airspace "is becoming completely unsafe" for civil aviation."We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That's why we are warning our partners: the days of safety in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said.Andriy Zagorodnyuk, a former Ukrainian defence minister, said the goal was not to attack civilian aircraft but to create lasting uncertainty."Ukraine is not seeking to shoot down civilian aircraft, but it is making Russia's skies unsafe for flying," he said in last week's comments to Ukrainska Pravda.The trigger for airport closures is the activation of what Russia calls the "Kover" — Russian for "carpet" — protocol, an air defence procedure designed for rare emergencies that grounds or redirects all civil aircraft when a drone threat is detected in the area.Military analyst Mykhailo Samus, of the Centre for Army, Conversion and Disarmament Studies, said airport closures were part of a broader strategy of economic exhaustion, alongside rising insurance premiums, the withdrawal of foreign carriers and reduced domestic mobility."Airport closures are the new reality for Russian aviation," he said.'Impossible to take off or land'Russia's Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said no significant disruptions to civil aviation would be allowed, yet operational data contradict his statement.In the first three days of September, an average of 86 flights per day were cancelled in Russia, according to FlightRadar24 — a level comparable to August's worst periods.On the most severe nights around Moscow, between 77 and more than 100 flights were delayed or cancelled in a single overnight period.Passengers have documented the disruption in detail on social media and in regional news feeds."We've been sitting on the plane for an hour, Vnukovo has been closed, nobody is explaining anything," one traveller wrote on Telegram."Pulkovo won't let the flight depart, Moscow won't receive it." another posted. A third passenger said, "The online board is all red, it's impossible to take off or land."Some foreign carriers that had continued to fly to Russia after the full-scale invasion have since adjusted routes or suspended operations.Changes have affected Pegasus, Flydubai and Air India, according to industry media.Passenger numbers on the Moscow-St Petersburg route have fallen by 20-23%, while rail demand has risen by roughly 20% in response.The investigative outlet Agentstvo has noted that the aviation disruption overlaps with pressure on other parts of the Russian economy, including declining oil refining capacity, higher logistics costs and interruptions to warehouse operations caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on industrial facilities.

US ambassador’s interventions in Greece spark controversy in Bucharest and Athens -Le Monde https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/10/04/us-ambassador-s-interventions-in-greece-spark-controversy-in-bucharest-and-athens_6758225_4.html Read it for free here: https://archive.is/siHpc According to revelations by the ‘Wall Street Journal,’ Kimberly Guilfoyle would not hesitate to threaten toppling governments to promote sales of American liquefied natural gas While the WSJ did not specify the reason, the ambassador reportedly mentioned the imminent fall of the Romanian government and said, “We can do that to any country we want. We can do it here.” Papastavrou is said to have replied that the US could not replace the democratically elected Greek government. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed this account, but that was not enough to put an end to the ensuing debate During the no-confidence vote, the PSD denounced “austerity measures” imposed by the Bolojan government. But political analysts had already mentioned “rumors” of American influence over the vote, citing disagreements between the Social Democrats and Bolojan on energy policy and relations with the “strategic partner,” the US. Three weeks after the Romanian government fell, the prime minister denied these claims, stating in his capacity as head of government and interim energy minister that he had not been subjected to any “pressure” to buy American gas. Yet, video footage and photographs released in the Romanian press have fueled suspicion. They show PSD leader Ivan and a presidential adviser, Nicusor Dan, alongside Guilfoyle at a dinner on the sidelines of a conference by British weekly magazine The Economist , held in Bucharest from March 30 to April 1, a month before the government’s fall. The ambassador’s presence is significant, as Greece has become central to the US energy strategy in southeastern Europe. “This vertical corridor is more than infrastructure; it represents freedom,” the diplomat declared at the conference Have a read for free. The Independent [UK] also picked up the story: https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/kimberly-guilfoyle-greece-trump-collapse-b3058278.html Well, I might give a pass, but for: Inside the unraveling of U.S. diplomacy under Trump -Reuters https://www.reuters.com/investigations/inside-unraveling-us-diplomacy-under-trump-2026-05-21 Read it for free here: https://archive.is/L6n2P Donald Trump’s threats, personal envoys and hollowed‑out U.S. embassies are reshaping Washington’s presence in the world. Allies from Europe to Asia are rewriting the rules of engagement – ignoring the president’s rhetoric and forging new diplomatic channels to manage a U.S. foreign policy driven increasingly by personalities, not institutions . LONDON – When Donald Trump warned Iran on April 7 that “a whole civilization will die tonight,” a European diplomat in Washington said his government wanted an urgent answer to a chilling question: Was the U.S. president contemplating the use of a nuclear weapon? Across Europe and Asia, the concern went beyond whether Trump’s apocalyptic threat was real or bluster. One fear, the diplomat said, was that Russia could seize the moment to justify similar threats in Ukraine, triggering a nuclear crisis on two continents. European governments immediately sought reassurance through a traditional channel: the U.S. State Department. But according to the diplomat, officials there gave an unsettling response: They didn’t know what Trump meant or what actions his words might portend. https://55krc.iheart.com/content/2026-10.text: Photo : Brandon Bell / Getty Images News / Getty Images Vice President Vance defended new television ads featuring President Trump , stating they are "not partisan" despite criticism from both Democrats and Republicans. The ads, funded by $20 million of taxpayer money, highlight Trump's calls to defeat socialism and communism, and claim credit for "the largest tax cuts in history" and the resurgence of American manufacturing. The Trump administration insists these ads are public service announcements, not campaign ads. Vance compared them to past government-funded ads, such as those for the Affordable Care Act under the Obama administration. He argued that the ads are about promoting the country's greatness, not political campaigning. President Trump also stated that the ads are meant to capture the "spirit of the country" and do not explicitly support any candidate. Critics, including Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin and Republican Senator Thom Tillis , argue that the ads violate the Hatch Act, which restricts government resources from being used for political purposes. Tillis likened the ads to tactics used by former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. The ads have aired on major networks like Fox News and CNN, drawing further scrutiny. Two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy , have demanded answers from the Department of Homeland Security about the use of funds for these ads. They argue that the ads are an inappropriate use of taxpayer money and have called for their removal from the airwaves. The Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr has stated that the ads are standard public service announcements and do not require FCC review. The debate continues as both sides prepare for the upcoming midterm elections.

Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters View image in fullscreen Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with US special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting in Saint Petersburg, Russia, 21 October, 2026. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia US envoy Witkoff presented Putin with proposals drafted by Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo earlier this week. What we know on day 1,702 Guardian staff and agencies Wed 21 Oct 2026 21.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 01.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Kremlin has criticised new peace proposals to end the war after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Commenting on the meeting, which followed talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway, the Kremlin warned there was little “substance” in the Ukrainian and European proposals. Despite the lukewarm response from Russia, US president Donald Trump claimed it was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. A day before travelling to Russia, Witkoff met Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo in a meeting aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between the Ukrainian president and Trump. Commenting on the Witkoff-Putin meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” the trilateral talks in mid-November – after crucial US midterm elections – and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on postwar security. Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on “some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, but added that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”. Zelenskyy said Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks as soon as possible. Witkoff said his talks with Putin were “constructive” but that “there is still important work left to do” . Discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added. However, the US envoy has face sharp criticism at home for describing Putin as a “humanitarian” , after the Russian leader agreed to free US citizen Stephen Hubbard from a Russian prison. US Republican senator Thom Tillis posted on X: “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian’.” Trump brushed off Witkoff’s comments, saying “I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other”, while US vice-president JD Vance said: “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.” Later, after a Russian ​strike on ⁠Kyiv that ​followed the talks, Ukrainian foreign minister ⁠Andrii Sybiha said that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russia’s war. Putin’s order to release Hubbard as he met Witkoff appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections, writes Pjotr Sauer . Trump had previously asked Putin to free Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Trump said on social media: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.” Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of ⁠Thursday and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight , authorities said, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks ⁠despite the latest ⁠US mediation attempts. The Russian strikes wounded 15 people and damaged subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in the Ukrainian ⁠capital while also restricting traffic there, Kyiv authorities said. The strikes came after another attack on the city on Wednesday evening that wounded six people. In Ukraine’s north-east, a Russian strike ⁠killed a woman and injured another four people in the Kharkiv region, governor ​Oleh Syniehubov said. And a drone hit energy infrastructure in ‌the Kremenchuk area in the Poltava region, a local official said. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow after 630 drones were sent towards the capital during the night, mayor Sergei Sobyanin ‌said. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added. US secretary of state Marco Rubio said decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were ⁠up to its parent company ⁠SpaceX and Elon Musk, ​not the White House , comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv’s access to the service. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade ⁠version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said the US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes after the Norway meeting with Witkoff.
